title: What Happened to School 21 and Oracy?
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Salles uses School 21, once feted for its oracy curriculum, as a case study in choosing a morally appealing idea over evidence. He points to the school's drop to Requires Improvement and its poor Progress 8 figures, including weak results for EAL students who should benefit most from an oracy approach. His explanation is that oracy is inefficient: talk is time-intensive and competes with the reading and writing that strong speakers need, which hurts the most able in particular. He extends the point to Voice 21 and to Research Schools, arguing educators adopt ideas that match their moral outlook without considering scale, failure modes or impact. The closing demand is simple: try what you like, but measure the difference and adjust. The bucket is Learning & Curriculum because the argument concerns curriculum choices and evidence of their impact.
points: The case against oracy rests on efficiency: time spent on talk is taken from reading and writing, with the most able losing most.
EAL students, the supposed proof case for oracy, scored far below national EAL progress at School 21.
Moral purpose is not a substitute for impact evidence, and the warning signs were in public performance tables.
The practical rule is to measure the effect of any new curriculum idea and adjust accordingly.
quotes: It shows how we will choose a fantasy over the evidence. The evidence that School 21 was failing was in the performance tables, for anyone who cared to look.

It is because we seek out ideas which agree with our moral perspective and leave it at that. We fail to consider how to scale it. We fail to anticipate all the ways it is going wrong. We even fail to look at the evidence of impact.
A student whom we teach to be brilliant at writing and reading, will have all the tools to be a great speaker. (All that may be missing is the ability to perform for an audience).
Moreover, this is actually more likely, because speaking is time intensive. The time you spend on this in the curriculum stops you improving reading and writing.
The better the oracy curriculum, the more progress EAL students would make from their starting points. EAL students had a progress 8 of -0.15. Nationally, they achieve +0.51.
But this is what you must also do. Measure that difference. Check to see what impact your idea is having. Adjust accordingly.
